motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of efficiently calibrating ensemble prediction intervals via split conformal methods that achieve robust finite-sample coverage despite distribution shifts interacting with ensemble heterogeneity. The central question is how to maintain coverage guarantees when distribution shifts interact with ensemble heterogeneity, given existing gaps in split conformal calibration. Supporting evidence indicates a gap of 1/(n + 1) explains why empirical coverage (89.1% with n = 200) is close to but slightly below the 90% target. Additionally, fluctuations arise from the finiteness of nval, the size of the validation set. While EnbPI avoids data-splitting and is computationally efficient by avoiding retraining, scalability remains a consideration for sequentially producing prediction intervals. A possible approach is to investigate mechanisms connecting independent gaps to improve calibration robustness. A successful outcome would provide clearer understanding of coverage fluctuations under distribution shifts. This would clarify the tradeoff between computational efficiency and statistical robustness in ensemble settings. This project would investigate methods to address the unresolved tradeoff between split conformal limitations and ensemble heterogeneity.
problem_statement: The problem of efficiently calibrating ensemble prediction intervals via split conformal methods that achieve robust finite-sample coverage despite distribution shifts interacting with ensemble heterogeneity.
title: Split Conformal Prediction

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing single-pass conformal prediction systems that achieve robust coverage under distribution shift despite the computational cost of ensemble-based calibration required for statistical validity. The central question is how to resolve computational cost conflicts that achieve robust coverage under distribution shift despite the reliance on ensemble-based calibration for statistical validity. Supporting evidence indicates that ensemble methods require training multiple instances, multiplicatively increasing the already substantial computational cost of eigendecomposition operations. Furthermore, MC dropout is computationally expensive for larger networks and only captures epistemic uncertainty. Directly computing determinants of Jacobians is also computationally expensive. In contrast to sampling-based uncertainty quantification methods, single deterministic approaches do not require multiple forward passes at inference time. However, its application is often limited by computational cost. A possible approach is to develop shift-robust, single-pass conformal prediction systems. A successful outcome would provide a method that balances validity with efficiency. This would clarify the tradeoff between ensemble reliance and inference speed. The project would investigate mechanisms linking ensemble reliance to shift robustness to address the cost ambiguity.
problem_statement: The problem of designing single-pass conformal prediction systems that achieve robust coverage under distribution shift despite the computational cost of ensemble-based calibration required for statistical validity.
title: Shift-robust, single-pass conformal prediction systems.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing a unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness. The central question is how to achieve information-theoretic optimality despite simultaneous structural non-stationarity and heavy-tailed noise. Existing approaches often assume context sets are generated i.i.d. from a distribution p, or that realized payoffs are normal random variables. However, the mechanism indicates structural non-stationarity amplifies heavy-tailed noise sensitivity, invalidating standard probabilistic exploration guarantees required for information-theoretic lower bounds. A possible approach is to integrate structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness to address these conflicting conditions. This would clarify the limits of exploration under shared unrealistic assumptions found in existing work. A successful outcome would provide a framework for robust exploration where standard guarantees fail. This project would investigate the feasibility of such an algorithm given the current gap in partial-feedback exploration. The proposed contribution type aims to resolve the assumption mismatch and shared failure condition inherent in current models. This work does not claim to prove optimality but seeks to establish the conditions under which such an algorithm might function effectively.
problem_statement: The problem of designing a unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness that achieves information-theoretic optimality despite simultaneous structural non-stationarity and heavy-tailed noise.
title: A unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing robust few-shot in-context learning strategies under parameter-efficient fine-tuning that maintain consistent task Lipschitz continuity despite ordering-induced Softmax geometric instability exacerbated by frozen weight constraints. The central question is how demonstration ordering disrupts the stationary distribution assumption, causing task Lipschitzness to vary and triggering Softmax geometric instability that LoRA's low-rank updates fail to regularize due to frozen weight constraints. While existing work considers linear MoR models where independent and identically distributed samples are assumed to follow the model, and since the Markov chain is initialized at its stationary distribution, this project would investigate the gap where ordering-induced Lipschitz instability triggers attention collapse despite LoRA-induced normalization perturbations. A possible approach is to analyze how noisy annotations significantly hurt the performance of in-context learning and whether this effect reverses when learning about counterfactual feedback. ICL can become transient in an asymptotic training regime. A successful outcome would provide a framework for robust few-shot in-context learning with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This would clarify the relationship between demonstration ordering and attention collapse under frozen weight constraints.
problem_statement: The problem of designing robust few-shot in-context learning strategies under parameter-efficient fine-tuning that maintain consistent task Lipschitz continuity despite ordering-induced Softmax geometric instability exacerbated by frozen weight constraints.
title: Few-shot in-context learning with parameter-efficient fine-tuning

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies self-verification mechanisms within test-time compute scaling frameworks. The central question is how to maintain accuracy when verifiable correctness assumptions collapse on inherently unverifiable intermediate steps. Current approaches often focus on complex problem-solving tasks where correctness is easily verified on labeled datasets. However, reliance on task-specific few-shot examples can limit generalizability across diverse tasks. Furthermore, existing methods fail to utilize negative samples for implicit exploration and do not improve on out-of-distribution tasks through experiments. The mechanism involves self-verification attempting to correct linear error accumulation inherent in Chain-of-Thought structures. Yet, this relies on assumptions that collapse when intermediate steps are unverifiable. This project would investigate verification-dependent error accumulation that achieves accuracy saturation despite increased inference-time search depth. A possible approach is refining these mechanisms to handle unverifiable steps without saturation. A successful outcome would provide insights into scaling frameworks. This would clarify the relationship between search depth and verification limits. The proposed contribution type focuses on self-verification mechanisms within test-time compute scaling frameworks. This work aims to address the unrealistic assumption that intermediate steps remain verifiable under increased compute scaling.
problem_statement: The problem of understanding self-verification mechanisms within test-time compute scaling frameworks that achieve accuracy saturation despite increased inference-time search depth due to the collapse of verifiable correctness assumptions on inherently unverifiable intermediate steps.
title: Self-verification mechanisms within test-time compute scaling frameworks.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of quantifying LoRA-mediated in-context learning robustness that achieves apparent stability despite the masking of low-rank induced induction head fragility by sparse evaluation of counterfactual context windows. The central question is whether current evaluation protocols adequately capture the stress interaction between non-IID context windows and low-rank constrained induction heads. A possible approach is to investigate how sparse evaluation fails to reveal specific stress interactions inherent to counterfactual feedback. This project would investigate the mechanism where non-IID context windows generated by counterfactual feedback specifically stress the low-rank constrained induction heads. A successful outcome would provide a clearer understanding of the theory-practice gap regarding LoRA-adapted transformer models performing in-context learning. This would clarify the extent to which apparent stability masks underlying fragility. The feasibility of this work is estimated at 0.72. This research aims to address the assumption mismatch and conflicting claims found in existing literature regarding induction head fragility. By focusing on the remaining gap scope, this study seeks to establish a more robust framework for evaluating LoRA-mediated models.
problem_statement: The problem of quantifying LoRA-mediated in-context learning robustness that achieves apparent stability despite the masking of low-rank induced induction head fragility by sparse evaluation of counterfactual context windows.
title: LoRA-adapted transformer models performing in-context learning.

problem_statement: The problem of designing a unified robust linear contextual bandit algorithm that achieves stable posterior concentration and bounded regret despite simultaneous violation of conditional sub-Gaussianity and Lipschitz dynamics under adversarial poisoning.
title: A unified robust contextual bandit framework.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the design of alignment-aware coverage validation mechanisms for offline Q-learning. The central question is how to certify robustness claims by quantifying unobserved online reliance despite unverified partial coverage assumptions masking interaction costs. Current approaches often abandon the strong full coverage assumption, instead assuming partial coverage. However, in practice, it is rarely realistic to assume that the offline data covers the entire state-action space. This project would investigate resolving conflicting robustness claims via alignment-aware coverage validation. A possible approach is utilizing alignment-aware coverage validation functions as a proxy for measuring unobserved online reliance. This would bridge the gap between data coverage gaps and algorithmic robustness claims. A successful outcome would provide offline Q-learning evaluation and algorithm certification frameworks. This would clarify the tradeoffs between data availability and algorithmic safety. The feasibility of this work is estimated at 0.73. This proposal addresses unresolved tradeoffs regarding sparse evaluation and conflicting claims in the literature. It aims to establish rigorous standards for validation in environments where interaction costs remain hidden.
problem_statement: The problem of designing alignment-aware coverage validation mechanisms for offline Q-learning that certify robustness claims by quantifying unobserved online reliance despite unverified partial coverage assumptions masking interaction costs.
title: Offline Q-learning evaluation and algorithm certification frameworks.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing a unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating drift-aware structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness. The central question is how to achieve sub-linear regret despite heavy-tailed noise masking drift-induced misspecification. While context sets are often generated i.i.d. from a distribution p, structural non-stationarity induces effective model misspecification that heavy-tailed noise obscures. This project would investigate distinguishing non-stationary drift from model misspecification within partial feedback settings. A possible approach is joint regularization for both drift and tail robustness. Existing methods like Thompson sampling assume a prior distribution for the unknown mean, and realized payoffs are often modeled as normal random variables. However, this work addresses scenarios where these assumptions may not hold. We make the technical assumption that the set of actions A is compact to facilitate analysis. A successful outcome would provide a mechanism where structural non-stationarity does not compromise performance. This would clarify the conditions under which Nash equilibrium concepts remain robust in non-stationary environments. The proposed contribution type is a unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating drift-aware structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness. This work aims to address the gap where heavy-tailed noise masks drift-induced misspecification.
problem_statement: The problem of designing a unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating drift-aware structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness that achieves sub-linear regret despite heavy-tailed noise masking drift-induced misspecification.
title: A unified partial-feedback algorithm integrating drift-aware structural regularization with heavy-tailed robustness.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing high-dimensional preconditioned conformal prediction methods that achieve valid single-pass inference in non-exchangeable settings despite the compounding calibration drift induced by high-dimensional distributional shifts. The central question is how to maintain valid uncertainty quantification in high-dimensional non-exchangeable settings via training-time preconditioning despite the compounding calibration drift of high-dimensional shifts. A possible approach is training-time preconditioning of model stochasticity, which mitigates high-dimensional calibration drift, enabling valid single-pass inference without ensemble diversity. Current limitations suggest dropout rates are not adjusted based on training data, and single deterministic approaches do not require multiple forward passes at inference time compared to sampling-based UQ methods. However, existing gaps such as 1/(n + 1) explain why empirical coverage remains close to but slightly below the 90% target, and fluctuations arise from the finiteness of the validation set size. A successful outcome would provide a framework for High-Dimensional Preconditioned Conformal Prediction. This would clarify the tradeoff between inference efficiency and calibration validity in high-dimensional shifts. The feasibility of this mechanism is 0.64625, requiring further investigation into validation set finiteness effects.
problem_statement: The problem of designing high-dimensional preconditioned conformal prediction methods that achieve valid single-pass inference in non-exchangeable settings despite the compounding calibration drift induced by high-dimensional distributional shifts.
title: High-Dimensional Preconditioned Conformal Prediction.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing uncertainty quantification methods that achieve rigorous coverage guarantees despite computational cost constraints inherent in adaptive calibration procedures. The central question is how to balance rigorous statistical guarantees with the substantial computational expenses often associated with current techniques. Supporting evidence indicates that ensemble methods require training multiple instances, multiplicatively increasing the already substantial computational cost of eigendecomposition operations. Furthermore, directly computing determinants of Jacobians is computationally expensive, and MC dropout is computationally expensive for larger networks while only capturing epistemic uncertainty. Consequently, the application of many existing approaches is often limited by computational cost. A possible approach is to investigate adaptive calibration procedures that mitigate these expenses without sacrificing coverage guarantees. A successful outcome would provide a framework for efficient uncertainty quantification. This would clarify the trade-offs between computational feasibility and statistical rigor in adaptive settings. This project would investigate methods that address the implicit conflict on computational cost across existing literature to resolve the identified gap.
problem_statement: The problem of designing uncertainty quantification methods that achieve rigorous coverage guarantees despite computational cost constraints inherent in adaptive calibration procedures.

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the quantification of LoRA's low-rank updates that achieve stable attention dynamics despite the geometric instability of Softmax attention when task Lipschitzness varies under non-IID few-shot initialization. The central question is whether LoRA's sparse evaluation across datasets masks whether its low-rank updates can compensate for the geometric instability of Softmax attention when task Lipschitzness varies. Current literature assumes independent and identically distributed samples and stationary distribution initialization, yet evidence suggests transformers fail to predict well especially with Ntrain = 5. Furthermore, smaller Ntrain does not provide sufficient sample size to recover the probability distribution well. This project would investigate how task Lipschitzness varies under these conditions. A possible approach is to analyze the mechanism where LoRA's sparse evaluation masks compensation capabilities. A successful outcome would provide clarity on the theory-practice gap regarding Transformer assumptions. This would clarify the extent to which idealized assumptions break under general graph variable 3. The feasibility is moderate, aiming to address the assumption mismatch and unrealistic assumptions inherent in current models.
problem_statement: The problem of quantifying LoRA's low-rank updates that achieve stable attention dynamics despite the geometric instability of Softmax attention when task Lipschitzness varies under non-IID few-shot initialization.
title: Transformer

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the discrepancy between observed LoRA adaptation performance on Linear Transformers and theoretical constraints regarding attention window adaptation and depth handling. The central question is how LoRA parameters inadvertently compensate for Linear Attention's structural rigidity, masking the theory-practice gap until distribution shift exposes limitations. Existing literature assumes Concat tokenization and relies on commutativity assumptions to characterize in-context mappings, yet notes that nonlinear link functions prevent single-index target learning. Despite these theoretical barriers, empirical evidence suggests high few-shot performance persists. A possible approach is to investigate whether LoRA parameters mask the inability to adapt attention windows and handle depth greater than 2. This project would investigate the mechanism by which LoRA adaptation succeeds where standard Linear Attention fails theoretically. A successful outcome would provide insight into the conditions under which LoRA parameters compensate for structural rigidity. This would clarify the remaining gap between theoretical assumptions and practical performance in few-shot settings. The study aims to resolve the assumption mismatch and missing stress test regarding depth and windowing.
problem_statement: The problem of understanding LoRA adaptation on Linear Transformers that achieves high few-shot performance despite Linear Attention's theoretical inability to adapt attention windows and handle depth greater than 2.
title: LoRA adaptation on Linear Transformers

motivation_or_abstract: This project studies the problem of designing a training-time exchangeability preconditioned conformal prediction method that achieves valid coverage guarantees with minimal calibration data despite non-exchangeable distribution shifts. The central question is how to achieve valid coverage with minimal calibration samples despite non-exchangeable distribution shifts and ensemble-free inference. A possible approach is training-time exchangeability preconditioning, which aligns model stochasticity to reduce the calibration burden required for valid coverage under distribution shift. This would clarify the relationship between model stochasticity and calibration efficiency in shift-robust settings. Current evidence suggests a gap of 1/(n + 1) explains why empirical coverage often falls slightly below targets, such as 89.1% with n = 200 versus a 90% target. Additionally, fluctuations arise from the finiteness of the validation set size. In contrast to sampling-based uncertainty quantification methods, single deterministic approaches do not require multiple forward passes at inference time. A successful outcome would provide a Calibration-Efficient Preconditioned Conformal Prediction framework. This would clarify the tradeoff between calibration-data efficiency and robustness against non-exchangeable shifts without relying on ensemble-free inference limitations.
problem_statement: The problem of designing a training-time exchangeability preconditioned conformal prediction method that achieves valid coverage guarantees with minimal calibration data despite non-exchangeable distribution shifts.
title: Calibration-Efficient Preconditioned Conformal Prediction.
